stories.topic: From Letters to the Royal Society, and Back Again
stories.summary: Ajay traces how research communication began. Scientists wrote a letter to the Secretary of the Royal Society in London describing their new work. The Secretary gathered these into a publication sent to all members, and modern journals grew out of that habit. Journals existed to disseminate research. Today that job has vanished: mature working papers, blog posts and newspaper pieces carry high-quality novel knowledge, and nobody needs a journal website to read a paper. What journals still provide is a brand name that helps you get a job or a grant.
stories.insight: Institutions outlive their original purpose and turn into credential machines. Once you see that journals now certify careers rather than spread knowledge, you can judge a paper on its merits instead of by where it was published. We are back to an everyone-to-everyone model, minus the Secretary.
stories.quote: Today the dissemination function is 100% gone. You never need to go to the journal website to get the paper.

stories.topic: SEC Trivia Gets Published, SEBI Drama Gets Rejected
stories.summary: Ajay describes the nightmare Indian social scientists face with global journals: 'this is not an interesting question.' Any obscure regulation change at the US SEC is thought worthy of the top finance journals. The dramatic regulatory moves of SEBI, arguably the world's most activist financial regulator, are dismissed because it is India. Indian researchers end up contorting their work to show it sheds light on 'the grand questions of the age as seen in Germany.'
stories.insight: Universalism can be provincialism in disguise. Ajay's alternative is to find the important questions in the reality you actually live in. That is where the energy and emotional resilience come from to survive setbacks and produce real discoveries.
stories.quote: I think that we should open the windows of our house and look out at the reality and identify the great questions of the age as we see them in our reality and our lived experience.

stories.summary: Recalling a fact from the Outlaws episode, Ajay notes that Mendel ordered forty copies of his paper from the press. Today there is no limit on copies because everything is electronic, but the world is now flooded with rubbish. A researcher who puts a finished paper on a website finds that nobody is waiting to read it.
stories.insight: The bottleneck has moved from printing copies to winning attention. Pushing your work out after it is written (videos, blog posts, op-eds, talks) is part of the craft, not vanity. Without it, Ajay jokes, YouTubers a hundred years from now will celebrate the paper nobody read in your lifetime.
stories.quote: At the same time, the world is deluged with too much rubbish.

stories.topic: The Cute Title That Kept Luring Ajay Back
stories.summary: Ajay admits that one paper's title (he won't name it or its authors) stuck in his head for years and pulled him back to read the paper several times. Each time, the paper turned out to be unrelated to the title. He thinks academia has overdone cute titles. Two that get the balance right: Vijayendra Rao's dowry paper 'The Rising Price of Husbands', which Amit loves, and Ajay's own paper with Ayush and Susan, 'But Clouds Got in My Way', about clouds blocking infrared radiation on its way to satellites.
stories.insight: The title is the one sentence most people will ever read of your paper. A literary flourish helps, but a title that doesn't describe the paper wastes the reader's attention and your credibility.
stories.quote: titles should not just be cute, they should also be about the paper.

stories.summary: Amit points out that Ajay's most frequent co-author is Susan Thomas. Ajay explains that people assume 'Shah and Thomas' means he is the lead author. In fact the papers list authors alphabetically, and her role is in no way smaller. He notes that alphabetical ordering is not universal and conventions differ by community. He likes it because the only real question becomes whether you get authorship at all. Once you do, everyone is equal, which avoids endless fights over the n-factorial possible orderings.
stories.insight: A good convention removes a fight people would otherwise have, here over status among co-authors. It also means you shouldn't read hierarchy into author order without knowing the field's rules.
stories.quote: Actually, it's just alphabetical, and you know, that's absolutely not the case that her work or role is in any way inferior to mine

stories.summary: After joking that alphabetical author lists hurt a 'Varma', Amit recalls research he learned about in Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers. People who reach the top in sports tend to be born in the first months of the year. Age-group cut-offs fall on 1 January, so a January-born twelve-year-old is more developed than a December-born one. That child gets selected, gets more practice, and the advantage compounds into adulthood.
stories.insight: Arbitrary cut-offs plus a feedback loop can turn a tiny head start into a lasting gap. It's worth asking where similar invisible sorting shapes who rises in any field, academia included.

stories.topic: Ajay Underestimated How Hard This Would Be
stories.summary: Looking back, Ajay says he started reading papers early. He assumed he would slide naturally from reading papers to writing them, and he was wrong. He has since learned by reviewing his own work from a year or two earlier. He also reverse-engineers papers that leave him 'shocked at how perfect' they are, asking how the authors pulled it off.
stories.insight: Reading a thing well does not mean you can make it. Learning a craft takes years, honest review of your old work, and studying how masters did it, not just what they concluded.
stories.quote: When I was young, I was a little too optimistic that oh it will be easy, I'll transition from reading papers to writing papers.

stories.topic: The World Didn't Pick Ajay's Best Papers
stories.summary: Amit asks how a creator handles work that gets ignored. He says he finishes an episode with full intensity, then forgets it and moves on. Ajay says his Google Scholar page shows that some papers got cited and many did not, and he doesn't think the world chose his best work. He accepts it: the archive exists and someone may find it in a hundred years. His enthusiasm for any paper decays exponentially, so he talks about a paper only while he is still excited by it. Right now that is his innovation-policy paper with Mashelkar and Susan Thomas.
stories.insight: You can't control how your work is received, but you can stay detached and keep moving. Let your own excitement decide what you promote, and never give a talk you don't want to give.
stories.quote: When I look at the list, I don't agree. I mean, I don't think that the world chose my good stuff.

core_ideas.explanation: Following Hayek and Keynes, Larry White compares ideas to timber. Abstract researchers grow the trees, applied researchers mill them into policy ideas, and journalists and intellectuals build the furniture (books, op-eds, commentary) that policymakers and the public use. Amit uses this as the starting picture and asks where today's pipeline has broken.
core_ideas.quote: High level economic researchers produce abstract ideas, which applied economic researchers turn into less abstract policy ideas, which journalists and intellectuals then embody in mass market books

core_ideas.concept: The End of the Physics Illusion
core_ideas.explanation: Social science once hoped for grand unifying theories that hold everywhere, the way physics does. The data revolution changed that. There are now roughly 10,000 important datasets, each its own universe with its own logic and its own small community of specialists (for example, the people who work on the CMIE household survey). Economics has become solving one puzzle at a time, loosely held together rather than loyal to one framework.
core_ideas.quote: It's better to be loyal to the reality rather than settle for a sweet abstraction.

core_ideas.explanation: Fields differ in how far their findings travel. Physics and mathematics are fully universal. The humanities are fully contextual. Social science sits in between, needing deep local context while drawing on general theory. Even STEM can turn local: diabetes in India might differ from diabetes in China if genetics matter.
core_ideas.quote: So I think that there's a spectrum of universality. At one end is physics, is mathematics, which are completely universal. At the other end are humanities that are completely contextual.

core_ideas.concept: A Paper Is a Unit of Knowledge, Not a Journal Credential
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay defines a 'paper' broadly: any piece of new insight, whether a blog post, op-ed, working paper or journal article. Knowledge is a graph of such papers feeding into each other, used by three kinds of decision-makers: individuals, firms and governments. Journals no longer spread knowledge; they hand out credentials. A mature reader can judge a paper directly: did it give me a new idea, did it change my mind?
core_ideas.quote: Journal publication is there for the sole purpose of credentials. I got a pub in this journal, please give me a job, please give me a grant.

core_ideas.explanation: Every STEM or social-science paper needs three things. It needs a clearly stated question, a persuasive and well-supported answer, and novelty. A summary of twenty existing papers, which an LLM could write, is useful but is not a paper. The same tests make a good referee report: the reviewer restates the question and the answer in their own words, then judges whether the claims are supported and whether the work is new. In a confused paper, neither the question nor the answer can be pulled out easily.
core_ideas.quote: So we should focus on three elements. What's the question? Is the clarity on the question? What's the answer? Is the answer persuasive? And a test. Is it novel?

core_ideas.concept: Importance Is in the Eye of the Beholder
core_ideas.explanation: Gatekeepers claim to know which questions matter. Global warming does; the headgear of tribals in Chandrapur doesn't. Ajay rejects this snobbery. Researchers guard their time carefully, so if someone has put serious effort into a question, outsiders should assume there are people and situations for which it matters. The establishment said the same dismissive thing to every maverick in history.
core_ideas.quote: importance is in the eye of the beholder. If you were actually embedded in that community in Chandrapur, It may well be that you think headgear is very important and global warming is not.

core_ideas.concept: How to Play the International Journals Game
core_ideas.explanation: If you want to publish in international journals, Ajay offers two pieces of advice. First, position your work around questions those journals already find interesting, for example a natural experiment in your country that sheds light on their world. Second, avoid big breaks with the past, because peer review rewards small, incremental improvements. Amit is blunter: in peer review the excellent are always judged by the mediocre. Both agree this has nothing to do with writing a good paper for its own sake.
core_ideas.quote: When you do large breaks with the past, the peer review chokes. So if you go to the peer reviewers with Mendelian genetics, they'll throw it out.

core_ideas.explanation: In his writing course, Amit asks why people who master difficult subjects still fail to communicate, even with friends or partners. His answer: learning involves one variable, yourself, while communication involves two, you and the other person. Writing is not transferring what's in your head onto a screen. It succeeds only when it has the intended effect on the intended reader.
core_ideas.quote: Communicating is tough because there are two variables, right? And most writers or most of us in communication make the mistake of ignoring the second variable.

core_ideas.explanation: Researchers like to think writing is for creative-writing people and cut corners on it. Ajay says the purpose of a paper is to change a skeptical reader's mind. That needs passion and prose that is lively and engaging; being an academic is no excuse for dullness. Most papers sink without a trace, partly because too little care went into writing them. In the old adage he quotes, if it was not hard to write, it will not be easy to read.
core_ideas.quote: writing a research paper is a lot more like writing than researchers care to admit.

core_ideas.concept: The Paper Is Not the Journey
core_ideas.explanation: Doing research is like climbing a mountain, with fumbling, dead ends, months away and sudden aha moments. The paper should leave all of that out and present only the question, the approach, what was done and what was found. The journey can also change the destination: you may set out for India and arrive in America, and then you write about the route to America. Amit's summary: while doing the work, it's the journey; when presenting it, it's the destination.
core_ideas.quote: They don't want to know your life story. They don't want to know your exploration.

core_ideas.concept: Learn the Structures, Then Break Them
core_ideas.explanation: Beginners should stick to standard structures and break them only once they have found their powers. The STEM default is IMRD. The Introduction reviews what is known and ends with your questions. Methods must be detailed enough for anyone to replicate the work. Results report the findings with little interpretation. Discussion explains what they mean and where research should go next. Ajay's economics version has a title and abstract, then an 'introduction' that is really a 1,000-word executive summary, often published separately. After that come the setting and questions, the methods and results, robustness checks against alternative explanations, and a conclusion that asks 'so what?'
core_ideas.quote: And then as you grow up, you find your powers, then you can smash the boundaries and do things in novel ways, but it helps to know structures.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's rule of thumb: about 100,000 people see the title, 10,000 read the abstract, 1,000 start the paper and 100 finish it. Better writing widens every stage. So the title, a one-sentence summary, and the 100-word abstract deserve the most care.
core_ideas.quote: So a hundred thousand people are going to read the title of your paper, so make it count.

core_ideas.concept: Write Inside Out, and Be Ready to Throw It Away
core_ideas.explanation: Writing changes what you think, so planning from the title down rarely works. Ajay writes the body first (setting, questions, methods, results), then the conclusions, then the 1,000-word introduction, then the abstract, and the title last. Writing is expensive, but don't hold on to text just because you produced it, since that is a sunk-cost trap. Ajay often deletes a weak chunk and rewrites it from scratch rather than patching old prose.
core_ideas.quote: because I find the mind is cleaner when writing from scratch, rather than tinkering with my old stuff.

core_ideas.concept: The Slideshow as a Development Platform
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's teams build the paper first as a dense internal slideshow of 40 to 50 slides, containing every table, graph and citation in the order the argument runs. Each meeting walks through it and produces errors to fix and new ideas. Assistants, who are apprentices, implement the changes and must come back with something they believe is flawless and are ready to defend. When meetings stop producing changes, the work has converged and is turned into prose. Amit separates this from Jeff Bezos's ban on simplifying PowerPoints: this deck holds everything and is never shown to an outside audience. Ajay also distinguishes the roles: authors invent, assistants implement and are thanked rather than credited as authors.
core_ideas.quote: So we should never take this slideshow and try to take it to an audience. This is just a development platform.

core_ideas.explanation: Finished work still needs pushing: blog posts, newspaper pieces, a video of the paper, and talks. Ten minutes in front of 200 people leaves no impression; 30 to 50 minutes with ten focused people actually changes minds. So Ajay avoids big conferences and goes to small ones. Amit links this to a line he borrowed from Paul Graham: it's better to be loved by a few than liked by many.
core_ideas.quote: intense engagement with a few people is much better than a shallow engagement with large numbers of people.

core_ideas.concept: Writing Papers Takes a Long Apprenticeship
core_ideas.explanation: Paper-writing is a craft, and you get better through practice, honest review of your past work, and studying how excellent papers were built. A PhD doesn't make you good at it. Being able to conceive a research project and lead it to completion takes many years after the PhD.
core_ideas.quote: So a sad fact of the modern world is most people who have finished a PhD are actually quite bad at writing papers.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens by promising that after his masterclass, 'gentle readers will become gentle writers.'

Ajay on research guiding individual choices: to decide whether to go to college, 'first you should get a PhD and learn to read the papers about the gains from college... Because if you haven't read those papers, how can you make a decision about whether or not it's worth going to college?' Amit: 'This is a trap.'

Amit, on Ajay's Chandrapur example: 'There is also the radical possibility that the headgear of the Chandrapur tribals causes global warming.' Ajay plays along with a straight face, suggesting obscure chemicals in the headgear could trigger reactions in the upper atmosphere. Amit: 'I didn't expect you to riff off my immature quip, but continue.'
Amit: 'I will say this as gently as I can. I think the peer review system makes me want to puke.'

Amit, after Ajay says journals only reward small incremental moves: 'You and I should throw a party where we call every academic we know and we get them completely drunk, and then we gather a bunch of journals and we have a bonfire of the journals.'
Asked why we fail to communicate, Ajay brings up Broca's area, the part of the brain that handles speech. Amit: 'That's a deeply technical answer and it is absolutely correct.'
Ajay mentions the Leap Blog without explaining it, and Amit catches him: 'You just committed the curse of knowledge.'
Amit pictures Ajay, Ayush and Susan finishing their exhausting paper, putting on Joni Mitchell, and finding the title 'But Clouds Got in My Way' in 'Both Sides Now.'
Ajay on deep engagement with a few people: 'This is why the universe created ten hour podcasts and one hour videos.'

Ajay on skipping self-promotion: a hundred years from now, famous YouTubers will make a show about the amazing paper you posted on the website of IIM Kozhikode, 'but nobody in this world bothered to read that paper.'

Amit's theory of alphabetical injustice: would he have written more papers if his name were Ahluwalia? Hayek, Friedman, Keynes and Arrow all sit early in the alphabet. 'There's no great economist called Zimbalist.' Ajay turns it into a research project: test whether the first letters of econ Nobel laureates' surnames differ significantly from the general population.
Amit, after the Outliers birthday effect, notes that his surname starts with V and adds: 'I'm born in fucking December. I had no chance.'
Amit says that if one phrase sums up the show Everything is Everything, it is 'the sociology of how this machine works.'

Karl Marx's epitaph, cited by Ajay to distinguish research that only seeks to understand the world from research meant to act on it: the philosophers have tried to understand the world; 'the point, however, is to change it.'

Ignaz Semmelweis, Mendel and Darwin from the Outlaws episode, which Amit uses as proof that path-breaking work would never get through peer review. On Darwin he adds the caveat 'unless Wallace was a peer.'
Georges Simenon, one of Amit's favourite novelists, who said the key theme of all his work is that no two people can ever communicate with each other.
The apocryphal apple falling on Newton's head, Amit's example of the kind of behind-the-scenes origin story that does not belong in the paper.
Blaise Pascal, quoted by Amit: 'I'm sorry this letter is so long, I did not have time to make it short.'
Joan Didion, quoted by Amit: 'I write to find out what I think.' He uses it to support Ajay's point that writing changes the argument as you go.
Jeff Bezos's rule at Amazon, 'do not bring me an effing powerpoint': people write full prose pages that everyone reads before the meeting. Amit contrasts it with Ajay's detailed internal slideshow.
Paul Graham's line, which Amit has adopted: 'It's better to be loved by a few than liked by many.'
